sections.figure_alt: A magnitude sketch that falls, then falls more steeply.
sections.body_md:
A feedback loop with a finite loop gain does not quite hit the gain the feedback path would set by itself. The fraction still missing is
\[ S = \frac{1}{1+L}. \]
When \(L\) is large, \(S\) is about \(1/L\) and the miss is small. When \(L\) is only a few, the \(1\) in the denominator matters and the shortcut \(1/L\) is visibly wrong. The complementary fraction \(L/(1+L)\) is the part of the ideal ratio the loop does achieve, and the two fractions add to \(1\).

\(L\) depends on frequency. It is usually large at low frequency and smaller after the loop gain rolls off. The miss grows on that same trip: a loop that is accurate on a slow signal is less accurate on a fast one. The number \(S\) is also the factor a later skill applies to an output disturbance and to a tracking error. This skill is the fraction itself.

sections.heading: Key equations
sections.body_md:
\[ S = \frac{1}{1+L}, \qquad \frac{L}{1+L} = 1 - S. \]
At a frequency where you only know the size \(|L|\), the size of the miss is \(1/(1+|L|)\) when \(L\) is real and positive. Infinite \(L\) at DC, the situation an integrator creates, makes the steady miss on a constant reference zero. A finite \(L(0)\) leaves the miss \(1/(1+L(0))\).

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.body_md: A loop has \(L = 16\) at low frequency, so the miss is \(1/17\), about \(0.0588\). At a higher frequency the same loop has fallen to \(L = 5\), and the miss is \(1/6\). The signal did not change the ideal feedback ratio. The loop gain got smaller, so a larger fraction of that ratio is missing. The shortcut \(1/16\) is close to \(1/17\). The shortcut \(1/5\) is not close to \(1/6\). Using \(16/17\) would report the part that was achieved, not the miss.

sections.heading: Common pitfalls
sections.body_md:
- Using \(1/L\) when \(L\) is only a few.
- Reporting \(L/(1+L)\) as the miss. That is the complementary fraction.
- Treating \(S\) as a DC-only number after \(L\) has been given as a function of frequency.
- Expecting the miss to shrink when \(|L|\) falls.

sections.heading: Where this leads
sections.body_md: The same \(S\) multiplies an output disturbance and a tracking error, and \(T = 1-S\) multiplies sensor noise. That reading is the next one. An integrator is one way to make \(L(0)\) infinite so the steady miss on a constant reference vanishes. An amplifier whose open-loop gain is finite leaves this same fraction as a gain error.
